title: What to plant
translation: The trees I'd want at home are pine and cherry. A five-needle pine is nice too. Cherries should have single blossoms. Double cherries used to grow only in the old capital at Nara, but lately you see them everywhere. The cherries at Yoshino and the one in front of the palace hall all have single blossoms. Double cherries are odd things, fussy and twisted. You don't need to plant them. Late cherries are dreary too, and the ones with insects on them are unpleasant.

Plums: white ones, pale pink ones, single ones that bloom early, and double red ones with a lovely scent. They're all good. The poet Teika used to say: "Late plums bloom at the same time as the cherries, nobody notices them, and they shrivel up on the branch. It's depressing. Single ones that bloom first and fall first are quick, and I like that." And he did plant single plums close to his eaves. Two of them still seem to be there, on the south side of his house on Kyōgoku.
Willows are lovely too. Young maple leaves in early summer are better than any flower or autumn leaf. Orange trees and katsura trees are best when they are old and big.

Among smaller plants: yellow kerria, wisteria, irises and pinks. Lotus in the pond. In autumn: reeds and pampas grass, bellflowers, bush clover, asters, gentians, chrysanthemums (yellow ones too), ivy, kudzu and morning glories. Keep them all low, on a small fence, and not too thick.

Anything else, rare plants with Chinese-sounding names that grate on the ear and flowers you don't recognise, doesn't appeal to me much. Things that are unusual and hard to find are nearly always what people without taste get excited about. You can do without them.

literal: The trees one would like to have at home: pine and cherry.
As for pine, the five-needle one is also good.
As for blossoms, single ones are good.
Double cherries existed only in the capital of Nara, but it seems that lately they have become numerous in the world.
The blossoms of Yoshino and the cherry of the Left Guards are all single.
Double cherries are strange things.
They are very excessive and twisted.
One can do without planting them.
Late cherries are also dreary.
Ones with insects on them are also unpleasant.
As for plums, white ones, pale red ones, single ones that bloom early, and double red ones with a splendid scent: all are delightful.

Saying 'Late plums bloom together with the cherries, their reputation falls, they are overshadowed, and they cling withered to the branch: it is depressing. Single ones that bloom first and fall are quick in spirit and delightful', the Kyōgoku lay monk Middle Counsellor still planted single plums close to the eaves.
On the south side of the house at Kyōgoku, two trees seem to be there even now.
Willows too are delightful.
Young maple leaves around the fourth month are splendid things, better than all flowers and autumn leaves.
Tachibana and katsura: for both, the trees are good when they are old and big.
As for plants: kerria, wisteria, rabbit-ear iris, pinks.
In the pond, lotus.

As for autumn plants: reed, pampas grass, bellflower, bush clover, patrinia, thoroughwort, aster, burnet, karukaya grass, gentian, chrysanthemum, yellow chrysanthemum too, ivy, kudzu, morning glory; all of them good when not very tall, on a small fence, and not dense.
Besides these, things rare in the world, with Chinese-sounding names that are unpleasant to hear, and flowers one is not used to seeing: these are not very appealing.
In general, things that are all unusual and hard to find are what people of no quality make much of.
One can do without such things.

notes.text: {五葉|ごえふ}: the five-needle pine (Japanese white pine), with its needles in bunches of five. Ordinary Japanese pines have two.

notes.quote: 八重桜は奈良の都にのみありけるを
notes.text: Double cherries were famous from a poem in the Hundred Poets anthology: いにしへの{奈良|なら}の{都|みやこ}の{八重桜|やへざくら}, 'the double cherries of the old capital at Nara'. Nara had been the capital until 784. なる after a verb here means 'I hear': Kenkō reports it.

Yoshino, in the mountains south of Nara, was the most famous place for cherry blossoms in poetry. The 'cherry of the left guards' stood in front of the main ceremonial hall of the palace, on the side where the guards of the left lined up; an orange tree stood on the other side.

notes.quote: いとこちたくねぢけたり
notes.text: こちたし: 'too much, overdone' (the 1925 edition: 'fussy'). ねぢく: 'to be twisted, warped'.

Fujiwara no Teika (1162–1241), the leading poet of his age and an editor of the Shin Kokinshū. He lived on Kyōgoku Avenue and ended his career as a Middle Counsellor ({中納言|ちゆうなごん}) who had taken vows. Kenkō, as a poet of the Nijō school, was in Teika's line.
{心疾|こころと}し: 'quick-minded, prompt'. Teika praises the early plum as if it were a person with good sense.

{卯月|うづき}: the fourth month, the start of summer in the old calendar. {若楓|わかかへで}: young maple leaves, fresh green. Maples are usually praised for their red autumn leaves; Kenkō puts the fresh green ones above everything.
{橘|たちばな}: a small wild Japanese citrus with white flowers and a famous scent. {桂|かつら}: the katsura tree, which also grows in the moon in Chinese legend.

notes.quote: 秋の草は荻、薄、桔梗、萩、女郎花、藤袴、紫菀、吾木香、刈萱、龍胆、菊、黄菊も、蔦、葛、朝顔
notes.text: The whole list: {荻|をぎ} reed, {薄|すすき} pampas grass, {桔梗|きちかう} bellflower, {萩|はぎ} bush clover, {女郎花|をみなへし} patrinia, {藤袴|ふぢばかま} thoroughwort, {紫菀|しをに} aster, {吾木香|われもかう} burnet, {刈萱|かるかや} a tall grass, {龍胆|りんだう} gentian, chrysanthemum, yellow chrysanthemum, ivy, kudzu, morning glory. Several of them are among the classic 'seven plants of autumn' from a poem in the Man'yōshū. The translation keeps the ones with familiar English names.
おの makes no sense here and is very likely a misprint in the 1925 edition for もの 'things', the reading of other texts. The translation follows もの.
